meta.title: Who really said "Why don't you come up and see me sometime?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Mae West said it — but not in that order. The line in She Done Him Wrong (1933) is “Why don’t you come up sometime and see me?” The familiar version blends two films.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Why don't you come up and see me sometime?'?
meta.ogDescription: Mae West said it, but not in that order. She Done Him Wrong (1933) has “come up sometime and see me”; I’m No Angel has “come up and see me sometime.”

answer.label: Misquoted — Mae West said it the other way round
answer.sourceLine: The words are West’s; the word order is not. In She Done Him Wrong (1933) she plays Lady Lou and tells Cary Grant’s Captain Cummings — the uniformed mission captain who turns out to be an undercover federal agent: “Why don’t you come up sometime and see me?” That is the version the American Film Institute ranked No. 26 among the great movie lines. The familiar “come up and see me sometime” ending is real too — West used it in I’m No Angel, released the same year — so the sentence people repeat is a splice of her two 1933 pictures rather than something she never said.

source.heading: What she actually says in the film

docMeta.dd: Lady Lou (Mae West), to Capt. Cummings (Cary Grant) — a fictional character
Harvey F. Thew and John Bright, from West’s 1928 play Diamond Lil

source.excerpt: I always did like a man in a uniform. That one fits you grand. Why don’t you come up sometime and see me? I’m home every evening.
trail: Wikiquote’s page for the film transcribes the line under Lady Lou ↗ as “I always did like a man in a uniform. That one fits you grand. Why don’t you come up sometime and see me? I’m home every evening.” The same page credits the screenplay to Harvey F. Thew and John Bright, based on the 1928 play Diamond Lil by Mae West.

Wikiquote’s Mae West page carries the same wording ↗ and notes that the line “has widely said to be misquoted with the paraphrase” “Why don’t you come up and see me sometime?” (the awkward phrasing is Wikiquote’s own).

Wikipedia’s article on the AFI list gives No. 26 as “Why don’t you come up sometime and see me?” ↗ and then lists that same entry in its Misquotes section, where the incorrect popular form is given as “Why don’t you come up and see me sometime?” That is the clearest statement we found that the circulating sentence is the wrong one.

Wikiquote’s page for I’m No Angel (1933) transcribes “And don’t forget. Come up and see me sometime.” ↗ and, later, “Come up and see me sometime — any time!” Wikipedia states the change directly ↗: West “changed it to ‘Come up and see me sometime’ in her next movie I’m No Angel, released the same year and co-starring Grant.” So both halves of the popular sentence are hers — they simply come from different films.
source.excerptNote: Wikiquote’s transcription of She Done Him Wrong (1933), with “see” italicised for emphasis in the original entry. Note the position of “sometime”: it falls before “and see me”, not at the end of the sentence.

sourceLink.text: Wikiquote: She Done Him Wrong (1933) — Lady Lou

source.rightsNote: She Done Him Wrong was released by Paramount in 1933, well after the 1931 cut-off beyond which US works are no longer in the public domain, so the film and its dialogue remain in copyright; screen writing is work-for-hire, which puts the rights with the studio rather than with West or the credited screenwriters. The single line is quoted here briefly for identification and commentary. We did not attempt to establish whether the sentence also appears in West’s 1928 play Diamond Lil, which would raise a separate and older rights question.

author.name: Mae West
author.heading: About Mae West
author.bio: Mae West (born Mary Jane West) entered vaudeville in 1907, at fourteen, and did not reach the screen until 1932 — a quarter-century on stage before Hollywood. Unusually for a star of her era she wrote much of her own material — including Diamond Lil (1928), the hit play that became She Done Him Wrong. Her screen persona ran on innuendo delivered too slowly to be missed, which made her both a censor’s target and one of the most quotable performers of the 1930s. The cost of being that quotable is visible here: her best-known line is remembered in a wording she never quite used.

misattribution.heading: Right star, wrong word order
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here — this is Mae West’s line, from a Mae West picture, delivered in the Mae West register. What drifted is the arrangement of six words, and the drift is so complete that the accurate version now sounds wrong to people who know the quote.

items.who: “Why don’t you come up and see me sometime?”
items.why: Not spoken in this form in She Done Him Wrong. Wikipedia’s AFI-list article files it under Misquotes ↗, alongside “Play it again, Sam” and “Toto, I don’t think we’re in Kansas anymore.”

items.who: “Why don’t you come up sometime and see me?”
items.why: Transcribed on Wikiquote’s page for the film ↗ and ranked No. 26 on the American Film Institute’s 100 Movie Quotes.

items.who: “Come up and see me sometime” — I’m No Angel (1933)
items.why: Wikiquote transcribes it in West’s next picture ↗, released the same year and also co-starring Cary Grant. This is why the misquote feels authentic: it is authentic, just reassembled.

misattribution.truthLine: West said both halves in 1933 — the question in She Done Him Wrong, the word order in I’m No Angel. The single sentence people quote appears in neither film ↗.

context.heading: Why this one drifted
lead: West came to Hollywood late and already formed. Wikipedia records her entering vaudeville in 1907 at the age of fourteen; she did not appear on film until Night After Night in 1932. When she did, she arrived with her own material: She Done Him Wrong is an adaptation of Diamond Lil, the 1928 play she wrote and starred in. It was made for $200,000 and grossed $2,000,000 domestically — a cheap picture whose dialogue reached an enormous audience, which is part of why its lines lodged so deeply in the language.

The misquote survives because West herself supplied the alternative. Having landed the line in one picture, she reused the shorter form in the next, and the two versions blurred in public memory within months of each other. A misquotation usually competes with a source; this one competes with the same performer saying it a second way.
detailsBody: The adaptation was contentious before a frame was shot. Wikipedia records ↗ that the Hays Office had declared Diamond Lil banned from the screen and demanded changes to strip out associations with the play, allowing the adaptation only on condition that the play not be named in publicity or advertising — which is why the film carries a different title from the work it is based on. Joseph Breen later blocked re-release in 1935 and again in 1949.
context.pull: The misquote feels authentic because it is authentic — just reassembled from two films.
